title: India's BrahMos Gambit: Why a ₹6,000-Crore Missile Deal With Vietnam Matters Far Beyond the South China Sea
excerpt: Defence Minister Rajnath Singh's Hanoi visit puts India's supersonic cruise missile at the centre of an Indo-Pacific chess game — and opens new doors for Indian defence exporters
body:
Defence Minister Rajnath Singh landed in Hanoi on Sunday for a two-day visit that could seal one of India's most strategically significant arms deals in recent memory. At the top of the agenda: the potential sale of the BrahMos supersonic cruise missile system to Vietnam, a transaction estimated to be worth nearly ₹6,000 crore (approximately $700 million) and one that would reshape the military balance in the South China Sea.

## The Deal on the Table

Singh is scheduled to hold bilateral talks with Vietnam's Minister of National Defence, General Phan Van Giang, with the BrahMos deal expected to dominate the conversation. Sources indicate that negotiations are in their final stages. If concluded, Vietnam would become the second international operator of the Indo-Russian missile system after the Philippines, which signed a ₹3,611-crore agreement in 2022.

The BrahMos — jointly developed by India's Defence Research and Development Organisation and Russia's NPO Mashinostroyeniya — is the world's fastest operational cruise missile, travelling at speeds exceeding Mach 3 with a range of over 400 kilometres. For Vietnam, whose maritime forces face the challenge of defending a 3,260-kilometre coastline against an increasingly assertive neighbour, the missile's ship-killing capabilities represent a qualitative leap.

## Context: A Partnership Decade in the Making

The visit marks the tenth anniversary of India and Vietnam's Comprehensive Strategic Partnership, recently upgraded to an "Enhanced Comprehensive Strategic Partnership" during the Vietnamese President's state visit to India earlier this month. The two countries signed 13 memoranda of understanding during that visit, spanning defence, trade, and regional security.

The BrahMos discussion builds on a Joint Vision Statement on India-Vietnam Defence Partnership towards 2030, signed during Rajnath Singh's previous Vietnam visit in June 2022. That roadmap outlined deeper cooperation in maritime security, defence manufacturing, and intelligence sharing — all of which are now bearing fruit.

India's own defence export ambitions have accelerated sharply. The government has set a target of ₹50,000 crore in defence exports by 2030, and BrahMos Aerospace — the joint venture that manufactures the missile — reported $500 million in revenue in 2025, driven substantially by international buyers. Several countries in Central Asia, South America, and the Middle East have reportedly expressed interest in acquiring the system.

## The Indo-Pacific Calculus

The geopolitical subtext is impossible to miss. Vietnam has been locked in a series of territorial disputes with China over the South China Sea's Paracel and Spratly Islands. Beijing has expanded its military presence in the region through artificial island-building and naval patrols. For Hanoi, the BrahMos offers a credible deterrent capability without the political baggage of purchasing directly from the United States.

For India, the deal advances its strategic objective of building a network of partnerships across the Indo-Pacific that can collectively counterbalance Chinese influence. Southeast Asian nations — including Indonesia, which is also in talks for BrahMos — are the critical middle ring of this framework.

Singh's itinerary underlines the point. After Vietnam, he will travel to South Korea from May 19 to 21 for discussions on defence manufacturing, regional security, and the inauguration of an Indian War Memorial commemorating India's role in the Korean War. The three-country sweep is India's most ambitious defence diplomacy push this year.

## What This Means for the Diaspora

India's evolution from one of the world's largest arms importers to a credible exporter of advanced weapon systems is a transformation that resonates deeply across the diaspora. For Indian-origin defence professionals, aerospace engineers, and technology entrepreneurs in Southeast Asia and beyond, the BrahMos export programme represents both national pride and professional opportunity.

The deal also strengthens India's hand in the Indo-Pacific region where millions of people of Indian origin live and work — from Singapore and Malaysia to Australia and Japan. A more assertive India in regional security architecture translates into a stronger diplomatic shield for diaspora interests.

## What's Next

Rajnath Singh is expected to pay tribute to former Vietnamese President Ho Chi Minh at the Mausoleum on the occasion of his 136th birth anniversary. The formal signing of a BrahMos agreement, if it happens during this visit, would be announced jointly. Even if the final signatures come later, the political will on both sides appears unmistakable. India's missile diplomacy has moved from aspiration to execution — and the implications will be felt from the Mekong Delta to Malabar Hill.
